    Trump Talks Ballroom & Arch After Election Loss
    Bloomberg's Jeff Mason joined the show to discuss the White House reaction to Republican midterm losses, President Trump's focus on the ballroom and Trump's acknowledgment that higher gasoline prices tied to the Iran war contributed to the defeat. He speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on Bloomberg’s Special Edition of "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Scudder Says Texas Is Not for Sale
    Kendall Scudder, Texas Democratic Party Chair, says Democrats' statewide wins in Texas were the result of people working hard over multiple election cycles and rebuilding the party's infrastructure. Scudder says Elon Musk got a tough message that "Texas is not for sale." Scudder says Texas is open for business, but communities should have a say in data center development instead of finding out after decisions have already been made. Scudder believes Democrats' priorities should include corruption reform, reducing property taxes and rolling back school vouchers while strengthening public schools. He speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on Bloomberg’s Special Edition of "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Panetta Says Voters Sent Trump a Message on Iran War
    Leon Panetta, former Secretary of Defense and White House Chief of Staff, says whether Susie Wiles remains White House Chief of Staff depends on her relationship with President Donald Trump, a relationship Panetta says appears to be good. Panetta says Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has little credibility with either Democrats or Republicans on Capitol Hill, has failed to keep Congress adequately informed and says Trump will eventually have to decide whether to keep him in the job. Panetta says Trump has to recognize that the American people have spoken clearly and do not support the war with Iran. He speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on Bloomberg’s Special Edition of "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Businessweek Daily: Dems Stage Midterm Sweep (Podcast)
    The people, companies and trends shaping the global economy. Watch Carol and Tim LIVE every day on YouTube: http://bit.ly/3vTiACF Riding a tide of voter angst, Democrats swept into power in Congress, with outrage over the cost of living and the war in Iran leading to a thundering rebuke of President Donald Trump and his party just two years after his dominant White House comeback. In a seismic political shift, Democrats’ strength suggested a breakdown of the coalition that delivered Trump a second term. The election results threaten to slow the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout, with policymakers potentially turning up the heat on increasingly unpopular data center projects. On today's episode: Joe Mathieu, Bloomberg 'Balance of Power' Co-Host Brody Ford, Bloomberg News Tech Reporter Nathan Dean, Bloomberg Intelligence Senior US Policy Analyst Joe Lovinger, Bloomberg News Texas Reporter (Source: Bloomberg)
    Democratic Sweep, Markets Rally & AI Stocks Slide
    The Close brings you the latest news and analysis leading up to the final minutes and seconds before and after the closing bell on Wall Street. Today's guests are Morgan Stanley Wealth Management Executive Director, Head of Policy & Geopolitical Strategy Monica Guerra, American Action Forum President Douglas Holtz-Eakin, Baird Senior Equity Research Analyst Michael Ha, JC2 Ventures Founder & CEO John Chambers, Scotts Miracle-Gro President & CEO Nate Baxter, Cantor Fitzgerald Asset Management Chief Market Strategist Eric Johnston, CFRA Research Senior VP & Equity Analyst Angelo Zino, 248 Ventures Chief Investment Strategist Lindsey Bell, Future Standard CEO Edwin Conway, & Host Hotels & Resorts CEO & President Jim Risoleo. (Source: Bloomberg)
    Republican Blame Game Starts as 2028 Hopefuls Angle for Position
    The Republican Party’s generational collapse in this week’s midterm elections ushered in a wave of finger-pointing largely aimed at the Oval Office, exposing deep fissures within the party and opening the door for 2028 hopefuls to hone their message.
    Canada, China Extend Tariff Deal, Aim to Boost Canadian Exports

The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop. Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets.     Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?
    AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here If your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarre mashups of popular video games. Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from. Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube for this informative video, which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more. Continue reading...  ( 18 min )
